title: Protect the service
intro: A public API is shared. One client in a tight loop, or one enormous request, can slow it for everyone else. This module covers the limits that protect a service, how to tell clients about them so they can behave well, and how caching removes work that never needed doing.

steps.title: Why limits are part of the design
steps.text:
Without limits, the capacity of the service belongs to whoever asks most. That is rarely an attacker. It is usually a client with a bug: a retry loop with no pause, or a job that requests every page as fast as it can.

A limit protects the other clients and the service itself. It is also part of the contract. A client developer has to know the limits to design around them, so publish every one: requests per minute, the largest page, the largest request body, and how long a request may run.

steps.title: Rate limits
steps.text:
A **rate limit** allows each caller a number of requests in a period, such as 600 per minute for each credential. Count per credential, not per network address, so that many users behind one office network are not treated as one.

When a caller goes over, answer `429 Too Many Requests` and say when to come back, with a `Retry-After` header giving the number of seconds to wait.

Better still, tell clients where they stand on every response, so that a well written client slows down before it is refused. Three headers are in common use for this: the limit, how much of it remains, and when it resets.

steps.title: How a client should retry
steps.text:
A limit only works if clients respond to it sensibly, so say what you expect of them.

- On a `429` or a `503`, wait for the time in `Retry-After` before trying again.
- With no such header, wait a little, then twice as long, then twice as long again. This is called **exponential backoff**.
- Add a small random amount to each wait. Otherwise a thousand clients that failed together all retry at the same instant and fail together again.
- Give up after a few attempts and report the failure.
- Never retry a 4xx other than `429`. The request is wrong, and sending it again will not make it right.

steps.title: Over the limit
steps.text: A client has used its 600 requests for this minute, with 20 seconds of the minute left. It sends one more.

steps.title: Other limits worth setting
steps.text:
| Limit | Answer when it is exceeded |
| --- | --- |
| Size of a request body | `413 Content Too Large` |
| Items in one page | Cap at the maximum, or `400` |
| Items in one batch request | `400` or `422`, saying what the maximum is |
| Time one request may run | `503` or `504`, and design slow work as a job, as the next module shows |

Set each of these before the first release. A limit that is added later breaks the clients that had been relying on its absence.

steps.title: Caching: the request you do not have to answer
steps.text:
The cheapest request is one that is answered from a copy. HTTP lets a server say how long an answer stays good.

`Cache-Control: max-age=60` means the response may be reused for 60 seconds without asking again. Add `private` when the answer is specific to one caller, so that a shared cache between the client and the server does not hand it to somebody else.

For data that changes at unpredictable times, use a **conditional request**. The server sends an `ETag` with the response, the same version marker used earlier for safe updates. The client sends it back in `If-None-Match`. If nothing has changed, the server answers `304 Not Modified` with no body. The client keeps its copy, and both sides have saved the work of sending it again.

steps.title: A dashboard that polls
steps.text: A wall display wants to stay up to date, so it sends this request once every second, all day.

steps.title: Exercise: limits for the tracker
steps.text:
The tracker is about to open its API to customers. Decide the following and note your reasons.

1. A rate limit, and what it is counted against.
2. The exact response when the limit is exceeded.
3. What a wall display that wants fresh data should do instead of requesting the full list every second.
4. One other limit you would publish.

Then continue.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. 600 requests per minute for each credential. It is generous for an interactive app and it stops a runaway loop within a second.
2. `429`, with `Retry-After` in seconds, the three rate limit headers, and the usual error body with the code `rate_limited`.
3. Request the list every ten seconds with `If-None-Match`. Most answers are then a `304` with no body. If the display needs changes at once, a webhook, covered in the next module, removes the polling altogether.
4. A maximum page size of 200 items, and a maximum request body of 1 MB.

The numbers matter less than the fact that they exist, are published, and are reported in a way a program can act on.

questions.prompt: Which response serves the client best?

choices.feedback: The service is working. A 5xx tells the client and your own monitoring that something is broken.
The status says the client is going too fast, and the header says exactly how long to wait.
The client would treat an empty list as a real answer and show the user that nothing exists.

questions.prompt: What is the best first improvement?

choices.feedback: That lets the waste continue. Nearly every one of those requests returns data that has not changed.
A smaller body helps a little. The request itself is still sent and answered 86,400 times a day.

choices.text: Use a conditional request and a longer interval
choices.feedback: With `If-None-Match`, an unchanged list costs a `304` with no body, and a ten second interval cuts the requests tenfold.
